# Air conditioning, ventilation, and respiratory virus transmission potential in South India

**Authors:** Palak Shah; Lauren Pischel; Brady Sack; KM Abdul Basith; Madolyn Rose Dauphinais; Komal Jain; Maria Florencia Martins; Sierra Wallace; Meagan Karoly; Subitha Lakshminarayanan; Chelsie Cintron; Sadhana Subramanian; Apratim Sahay; Kobto G Koura; Ralph Brooks; Sheela Shenoi; Palanivel Chinnakali; Pranay Sinha

## Abstract

Rising global temperatures are expected to increase time individuals spend in underventilated spaces and to increase transmission of respiratory pathogens. We studied the impact of ventilation on transmission potential and basic reproductive number (R0) of respiratory viruses in Puducherry, India.

We measured ventilation in thirteen homes and seven healthcare offices. We applied the Wells-Riley equation to estimate the transmission potential and R0 of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza under different ventilation conditions and viral shedding levels.

Viral transmission potential was high when doors and windows were closed and highest in the air conditioned (AC) condition. Transmission potential decreased significantly with natural ventilation. Rn equaled or exceeded 2 in the closed and AC conditions for medium and high virus shedders.

The transmission potential of respiratory viruses in underventilated homes and healthcare spaces is high, particularly with AC use. Natural ventilation does not reduce R0 below 1 for super shedders.

## Introduction

In South Asia, rising temperatures and intensifying monsoons due to climate change are projected to drive people indoors [1,2]. Poor ventilation, defined by the World Health Organization as spaces where air changes per hour (ACH) are less than 12, has been linked to higher airborne transmission of pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and tuberculosis [3].

Household adoption of air conditioners (AC) in India is also expected to quadruple by 2040 as incomes rise and heat extremes worsen [4]. Closing windows to operate AC recirculates indoor air and reduces airflow [5].

We evaluated how different ventilation conditions influence the transmission potential and basic reproductive number (R0) of two respiratory viruses with high pandemic potential, SARS-CoV-2 and influenza, in homes and healthcare settings in Puducherry, India.

## Methods

### Study design, population, and setting

We previously described our study design and population in our analysis of TB transmission [6]. Data was acquired from a cross-sectional pilot study conducted June-July 2024 in Puducherry, India. Ventilation measurements were taken in “finished” (constructed from improved materials) and “semi-finished” (constructed from rudimentary materials) homes of persons with tuberculosis (PWTB) and in finished healthcare spaces at a tertiary government hospital (Supplementary Table 1).

### Data collection

#### Carbon dioxide measurements

Air changes per hour (ACH) were measured using a carbondioxide (CO2) decay technique (Supplementary Methods) in three configurations: closed (doors/windows closed, AC and fans off), closed with AC, and open (doors/windows open, fans on, AC off).

#### Viral transmission probability calculation

We applied a modified Wells-Riley equation to estimate transmission probability of viruses [6]. We assumed the presence of one infectious individual per household, set pulmonary ventilation at 0.6 m3/h, and modeled a 10-hour exposure to reflect overnight contact or a typical workday.

We acquired quanta values for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza from the Airborne Risk Calculator, which compiled quantum generation rates for both viruses from multiple studies, including pandemic and non-pandemic subtypes of influenza A and influenza B [7]. We used quanta values at a resting activity level to model individuals sleeping at home or working quietly in an office at low, medium, high, and super viral shedding levels to represent the different rates at which individuals emit viruses. The quanta values for SARS-CoV-2 were 4.0 for low shedders, 15.8 for medium shedders, 28 for high shedders, and 142 for super shedders. For influenza, the corresponding values were 3.2, 35, 68, and 128. Rate parameters were calculated for each virus and shedding potential.

#### R0 estimation

We determined R0 through this equation: R 0 = P ( 1 − n ) where P is the Wells-Riley probability of infection, and n is the number of individuals in the space [8]. We assumed household and office occupancy to be 4.

#### Statistical analysis

We assessed normality and variance with Shapiro-Wilk and Levene’s tests and compared transmission potential between closed and open conditions across shedding levels with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.

## Results

### Study population

We conducted 45 measurements in 13 homes and 7 healthcare spaces in Puducherry, India (Supplementary Table 1). Of 13 homes, 9 were categorized as ‘finished’, and 4 as ‘semi-finished’ (Supplementary Table 2). Five spaces (one home and four healthcare) were equipped with AC.

### Viral transmission potential and R0 estimation

Natural ventilation significantly reduced transmission potential and Rn of SARS-CoV-2 in homes (Figure 2). Opening windows more than halved transmission potential for high (70.7%, SD: 19.2% vs 35.4%, SD: 12.1%; P < 0.001), medium virus shedders (60.6%, SD: 22.1% vs 24.2%, SD: 10.0%; P < 0.001), and low virus shedders (29.7%, SD: 19.7% vs 6.3%, SD: 3.5%; P < 0.001). However, potential remained elevated in the open condition for super shedders (72.2%). Mean Rn equaled or exceeded 2 in the closed condition for high virus shedders (2.12, SD: 0.57) and in both the closed and open condition for super shedders (2.74, SD: 0.23 and 2.16, SD: 0.32), respectively (Figure 1b).

Similarly, for influenza, transmission potential was high in homes in the closed condition for high virus shedders (84.1%, SD: 12.6%) and decreased significantly in the open condition (55.6%, SD: 12.4%; P < 0.001) (Figure 1c). Transmission potential was elevated in the open condition for super shedders (69.7%, SD: 10.4%). The Rn for influenza exceeded 2 in the closed condition for medium and high shedders (Figure 1d). For super shedders, R0 exceeded 2 in both the open and closed condition.

In healthcare spaces, natural ventilation substantially reduced transmission potential across all viral shedding levels of SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 2a). AC use did not change transmission potential for low shedders but increased transmission potential for super shedders (93.4%, SD: 1.8%), high shedders (74.0%, SD: 5.7%). and medium shedders (61.7%, SD: 7.0%). R0 exceeded 2 for super shedders in the closed (2.35, SD: 0.61) and AC condition (2.80, SD: 0.05), and for high shedders in the AC condition alone (2.22, SD: 0.17) (Figure 2c). Similarly, for influenza, transmission potential increased with AC use compared to the closed condition for super, high, and medium shedders (Figure 2b). R0 exceeded 2 at all viral shedding levels except for low with AC use (Figure 2d).

In the singular home equipped with AC, R0 exceeded 2 for high (2.24) and super (2.93) shedders for SARS-CoV-2 and for medium (2.36), high (2.63), and super shedders (2.79) for influenza. There was significant difference in transmission potential for both viruses at all viral shedding levels between finished and semi-finished homes in the closed condition (Supplementary Table 2). This was not observed in the open condition.

## Discussion

Our findings show that poor ventilation, particularly with air conditioner use, can elevate the transmission potential of respiratory viruses. These findings underscore the urgent need to implement ventilation as a crucial engineering control that protects against respiratory infections including novel variants of SARS-CoV-2 or influenza sub-types with high pandemic potential.

While natural ventilation remains the most effective and accessible strategy in many settings, it is not always feasible with rising temperatures, air pollution, or monsoon rains. Moreover, super-spreaders are a critical driver of transmission within populations, and our findings show that natural ventilation alone may be inadequate to prevent transmission. Supplemental mitigation strategies such as ultraviolet germicidal irradiation and Corsi–Rosenthal boxes offer scalable approaches to reducing viral burden in homes and congregate settings [5,9]. These tools complement existing infection-control strategies, particularly where mechanical ventilation is limited or increased AC use elevates risk.

Limitations to this study include a small sample size, including only one home equipped with AC, limiting the external validity of our results, especially in residential spaces. While this study provides valuable pilot data, larger studies are required to confirm these findings across seasonal variations in viral transmission and as household AC adoption increases in India. Second, the CO2 decay method used may overestimate ventilation as it assumes steady-state conditions prior to decay, which is difficult to obtain in large or leaky spaces. Finally, the q-values selected for these viruses were derived from multiple sources at different degrees of infectivity prior to 2022, and the transmission potential for SARS-CoV-2 may have undergone significant evolution since.

Future studies should examine how climate change alters exposure to poorly ventilated spaces and mixing behaviors in densely populated communities. Ventilation is a critical lever for reducing vulnerability to respiratory pathogens, particularly in households where the secondary attack rate of SARS-CoV-2 can exceed 10% [10]. Pandemic preparedness must therefore incorporate architectural design, improved ventilation, and emerging cooling strategies that do not compromise air exchange.
